clips.text: Your garden is screaming right now — dozens of times an hour, at the volume of a normal conversation. You can't hear a single one.
This is what your garden looks like to ears that can actually hear it.

In the next nine minutes: the lab that heard it, the farm that uses it, and the question nobody can answer. And it starts earlier than you'd think — with a walk you take every morning without hearing a thing.
It starts with a gift — one you should probably be careful what you wish for.
Tonight, while you sleep, someone hands you hearing that reaches a hundred kilohertz — five times higher than any human ear. Tomorrow morning, you walk into your garden.
The first thing you notice is that your garden is not quiet. It never was. A tomato plant by the fence is clicking — sharp little pops, thirty-five times an hour.

That's not a metaphor. Researchers in Tel Aviv measured it: a thirsty tomato clicks about thirty-five times an hour. A healthy one? Less than once. The difference between a thirsty plant and a happy one is the difference between a fire alarm and a library.
The clicks are loud, too — about as loud as a normal conversation. But they're pitched at fifty thousand hertz, and your old human ears quit at twenty.

So every garden on Earth is full of distress calls, and every gardener in history has been deaf to all of them. Think of every garden you've ever walked through. All that silence was an illusion — your ears were just tuned to the wrong station.
You crouch by the tomato. It sounds urgent. Three beds over, the basil is barely whispering. The succulent on the windowsill says nothing at all.
Each plant has a signature. Drought sounds different from a cut stem — one is a dry rattle, the other a sharp snap. You start learning the vocabulary before breakfast.
There is a cost to the gift, and you feel it by noon. Every stressed plant in the neighborhood is now your problem — a chorus of complaints you cannot switch off, only learn to live with.
And then you notice the strangest thing of all. The plants aren't just making noise. What if somebody out there is listening?
To understand what you're hearing, you have to visit the lab where a plant was first caught screaming — on tape.
March 2023. A basement lab at Tel Aviv University. Two researchers — Itzhak Khait and Lilach Hadany — seal a tomato plant inside an acoustic chamber and point ultrasonic microphones at it.

The microphones hear from twenty to two hundred fifty kilohertz — more than ten times higher than you. Then they stop watering the plant, and they wait. Acoustic foam swallows every echo. The only sound left in that chamber is whatever the plant itself is doing.
What comes back is not silence. Clicks. Pops. Little ultrasonic snaps — thirty-five an hour from the thirsty tomato, twenty-five from a freshly cut stem.

And here is the number that should unsettle you: at ten centimeters from the plant, those clicks hit about sixty-two decibels — the volume of a normal conversation. Sixty-two decibels is a conversation. Your tomato has been talking at conversation volume since before you were born — you just never had the ears.
Ten centimeters. Not across the room — close enough to lean in. Your garden has been holding conversations at conversation volume your entire life.
The paper estimates that an animal which hears ultrasound could pick up those clicks from three to five meters away. Your garden is not whispering. It is broadcasting.
Most of the sound energy peaks between forty and eighty kilohertz — fifty for the thirsty tomato, fifty-seven for the cut one. All of it above the twenty-kilohertz ceiling of human hearing.

The team fed the recordings to a machine-learning classifier. It could tell a drought-stressed plant from a cut one about seventy percent of the time. Not perfect. But far better than chance — and chance is all anyone had before March 2023.
Seventy percent is not a language. It's a hint — a suggestion that the clicks carry information about what's wrong. And a hint is all you need to start asking dangerous questions.
Because Hadany, the senior author, asked the one question nobody had asked: if the clicks travel through air, and they carry information — who might be listening?
But before the listeners — the farmers found something stranger.
So what makes the click? The leading hypothesis is almost disappointingly physical. The xylem is plumbing, not poetry — and plumbing, it turns out, can scream.
Inside every stem run the xylem — microscopic tubes hauling water upward from the roots.
Under drought stress, the water column snaps. An air bubble forms — then collapses.
That collapse is the click. Not a voice. A plumbing accident, amplified.
Hypothesis, not verdict. But it explains why thirst screams loudest — and why a cut stem snaps once, then goes quiet.

Now walk the gift into a wheat field in a dry year. The farmer doesn't need a laboratory — she needs to know which row is thirsty before the leaves curl. She walks the rows at dawn, the way farmers have for ten thousand years — except this time, the field is talking back.
With your ears, you'd hear it weeks early: the clicking rising from twenty-five to fifty an hour as the soil dries. An early-warning system with no batteries.
Think about what that replaces: soil probes, satellite maps, and a farmer's gut feeling — all outperformed by simply listening to the plants themselves.
Researchers are already training sensors to do what your gift does — ultrasonic ears in the field, listening for the stress chorus, watering only the rows that scream.

Precision irrigation by eavesdropping. Less water, same harvest — because the plants told you exactly when they were thirsty. Roughly seventy percent of the world's freshwater goes to agriculture. Listening could save a river.
But the farm is only the practical half. The strange half is still waiting in the dark — because something out there has been listening all along.
Back in Tel Aviv, two years after the clicks were recorded, the same labs asked Hadany's question properly. If plants scream in ultrasound — does anything answer?

Enter the Egyptian cotton leafworm — a moth whose females choose where to lay their eggs. In 2025, researchers gave them a choice: a box playing the clicks of a thirsty tomato, or a silent box. Spodoptera littoralis — the Egyptian cotton leafworm. A moth nobody writes poems about, about to make scientific history.
The moths chose the sound box. A distressed plant, heard but not seen, beat no plant at all.
Then the researchers neutralized the moths' hearing organs — tiny ears on their bodies — and the preference vanished. It was never the smell. It was the sound.
With two healthy plants to choose from, the females picked the silent one. A screaming plant, it turns out, is a bad nursery — stressed hosts make weak offspring.
The males got a control test — a generic ultrasound with no plant meaning behind it. They showed no preference at all. The females weren't reacting to sound. They were reacting to a message.
One species. Lab playback, not the wild. Egg-laying decisions only. But it is the first time anyone has caught an animal answering a plant back.
Not talking. Answering. The garden isn't a collection of silent objects — it's a room full of conversations you're not invited to.

And moths are just the beginning. Bats navigate by ultrasound. Mice hear it. Other plants may feel it as vibration. The night garden is crowded with ears. Three to five meters — that is the paper's estimate for how far the clicks carry to ultrasonic ears. Your whole garden is within earshot. Just not yours.

So here is the uneasy question your gift leaves you with. If a moth can hear a plant's distress and act on it — what does the scream mean? A moth the size of your thumbnail can hear a thirsty tomato and change where its children are born. You, with all your engineering, hear nothing.
Not pain. Plants have no nervous system, no brain, nothing that could feel. The click is physics — a bubble collapsing in a tube.
'Scream' is our word, not theirs. Journalists needed a verb; the truth needed a paragraph. But the shorthand stuck — because it feels true.
Does that make the scream a lie? No. It makes it a translation — our clumsy human word for a physical event we were never equipped to hear.
You wanted a superpower that would let you talk to nature. Instead you learned something stranger.
Nature was already talking — you were just deaf to it.
Tonight, walk into your garden and stand still. Somewhere in the dark, a tomato is clicking thirty times an hour at fifty kilohertz — holding a conversation at conversation volume.
Fifty kilohertz. Thirty times an hour. Sixty-two decibels at ten centimeters. Numbers don't make it poetic — they make it undeniable.
You will never hear it. Your ears top out at twenty kilohertz, and evolution never filed the paperwork to upgrade them.

Maybe that's a mercy. Because once you've heard the garden complain, you can never un-hear it. The gift was never really about the plants. It was about discovering how much of the world happens outside your senses.
If you could hear your houseplants complain — would you water them more, or wish you'd never asked? Tell us in the comments.

The science is real, and the uncertainties are honest. The clicks were recorded by Khait and colleagues at Tel Aviv University, published in Cell in March 2023. The moths answered back in 2025 — Seltzer and colleagues, eLife. What the clicks mean is still an open question — and that is the most interesting part.
